en: The Treatise on the Middle Way composed by Nāgārjuna.
Chapter One, titled "Examination of Conditions": Neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal.
It has neither manifold meanings nor diverse meanings; it is without coming and without going.
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, who taught dependent origination—the auspicious stilling of conceptual proliferation. (MŚ 1.2)
Neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause,
do any entities ever exist anywhere as having arisen.
There are four conditions: the causal condition, the objective condition, the immediate condition, and likewise the dominant condition; there is no fifth condition.
For the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities does not exist within conditions and the like;
since intrinsic nature does not exist, extrinsic nature (parabhāva) does not exist.
Action does not possess conditions, nor does action lack conditions;
conditions do not possess action, yet they do indeed possess action.
"These are indeed conditions because [the effect] arises in dependence upon them.
As long as [the effect] has not arisen, how could these not be non-conditions? (MŚ 1.7)
A condition for an object that is neither non-existent nor existent is not tenable.
Of what non-existent thing would there be a condition? And what purpose would a condition serve for that which already exists?
When a phenomenon is produced neither as existent, nor as non-existent, nor as both existent and non-existent,
how can a cause that produces it be logically tenable under such circumstances?
This existent phenomenon is taught as being without an object;
but if a phenomenon is without an object, how can there then be an object?
When phenomena have not arisen, cessation is not possible; therefore, an immediate [condition] is not logical. Furthermore, what could be the condition for that which has already ceased? (MŚ 1.11)
Since no existence is found for things that lack intrinsic nature,
the principle "when this exists, that comes to be" is simply not tenable.
And that fruit does not exist in the conditions either individually or collectively;
how could that which is not in the conditions come forth from the conditions? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 1.13)
If that [effect], though non-existent, proceeds from those conditions,
why does the fruit not also proceed from non-conditions?
The fruit consists of conditions, yet the conditions do not consist of themselves.
How can that fruit, which arises from things that do not consist of themselves, consist of conditions?
Therefore, an effect consisting of conditions does not exist, nor one not consisting of conditions;
since the effect is absent, how can there be conditions or non-conditions?
2. Examination of the Gone and the Not-Gone, the Second Chapter.
That which has been gone over is not being traversed; likewise, that which has not yet been gone over is not being traversed.
Apart from what has been gone over and what has not yet been gone over, the presently being traversed is not being traversed.
Where there is motion, there is going;

and since that motion exists in the process of being traversed (gamyamāna), and not in what has been traversed nor in what has not yet been traversed, therefore going exists in the process of being traversed.
How indeed could the going of that which is being gone over be possible,
when a double going upon that which is being gone over is not at all possible?
For one for whom there is a going of that which is being gone over,
it follows that there is a being-gone-over even apart from going, for that which is being gone over is indeed being gone over.
If there were motion in that which is being traversed, two motions would follow:
that by which it is being traversed, and furthermore, the motion itself within it. (MŚ 2.5)
If two acts of going were to occur, it would follow that there are two goers;
for indeed, an act of going is not possible apart from a goer.
If going is not possible apart from a goer, then how indeed will there be a goer when going does not exist? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 2.7)
First, the goer does not go; nor indeed does the non-goer go.
Apart from the goer and the non-goer, what third party could possibly go?
How indeed can it be tenable that "the goer goes," when a goer without the act of going is not at all possible?
For one who maintains the position that "the goer goes," it follows that there is a goer without going,
since you desire a going that belongs to a goer.
If a goer goes, it would follow that there are two acts of going:
that by which he is called a "goer," and that which he, being a goer, performs. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 2.11)
Going does not begin in what has already gone; it does not begin in what has not yet gone;
it does not begin in the process of going. Where, then, does going begin?
Prior to the commencement of going, there is neither a path being traversed nor a path already traversed; where could going begin? For how can there be going in that which has not yet been traversed?
When the commencement of going itself is not perceived in any way whatsoever, what is the gone, what is the being-gone-over, and what is the not-yet-gone that can be conceptualized? MŚ 2.14.
The goer does not stand still, nor indeed does the non-goer stand still;
what third party, other than the goer and the non-goer, could possibly stand still?
How could it be tenable to say that "the goer remains for so long," when a goer is not at all possible without the act of going? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 2.16)
Going does not exist in that which is being gone over, nor in what has been gone over, nor even in what has not yet been gone over;
the commencement and the cessation of going are the same as those of "going" itself.
It is not tenable that the going is the very same as the goer;
nor is it tenable that the goer is something entirely different from the going. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 2.18)
If the act of going were indeed identical to the goer, it would follow that the agent and the action are one and the same. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 2.19)
If, on the other hand, the goer is conceptualized as being entirely distinct from the act of going, then there would be going without a goer, and a goer without going. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 2.20)
For those two for whom establishment is found neither through identity nor through difference,
how indeed can their establishment exist?
By means of whatever going a goer is designated, that going he does not perform;
for there exists no one whatsoever who is preceded by going, since it is only someone [already existing] who goes.
By means of whatever going a goer is designated, he does not go by means of one other than that;
for it is not possible for there to be two goings, since he goes by means of only one.
One who exists as a real entity does not go in the three ways;
nor does one who does not exist as a real entity go in the three ways.
Going does not proceed in any of its three modes—as being existent, as being non-existent, or as both;
therefore, motion, the goer, and the destination do not exist.
3. Examination of the Faculties, the Third Chapter.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind—these six are the faculties; their respective spheres of activity are the objects of sight and so forth. (MŚ 3.1)
For seeing does not see itself;
since it does not see its own self, how will it see other things? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 3.2)

The analogy of fire is not sufficient for the establishment of seeing; that [analogy] has already been refuted along with seeing by means of the arguments concerning the traversed, the untraversed, and the being-traversed.
When there is no seeing whatsoever of anything that is not being seen,
how can it be logically consistent to say that "seeing sees"?
Vision does not see at all, nor does non-vision see;
by means of vision itself, the seer has also been explained—let it be understood in that same way.
There is no seer who exists apart from seeing, nor is there seeing apart from the seer. Since the seer does not exist, how can there be that which is seen and the act of seeing?
Just as the arising of a son is said to occur in dependence upon the mother and father,
so too is the arising of consciousness said to occur in dependence upon the eye and visible form.
Since there is no seeing of an object to be seen, the fourfold group beginning with consciousness does not exist;
how then can grasping and the subsequent factors come to be?
Hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind have already been explained.
One should understand the hearer, the object to be heard, and so forth, by means of vision alone. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 3.9)
4. Examination of the Aggregates, the Fourth Chapter. Form is not perceived apart from the causes of form; nor are the causes of form seen apart from form. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 4.1)
If form were devoid of the cause of form, it would follow that form is without a cause;
yet no object whatsoever exists anywhere that is without a cause.
If the cause of form were to exist independently of form itself, it would be a cause without an effect; yet there is no such thing as a cause that lacks an effect.
When form exists, a cause of form is not tenable;
when form does not exist, a cause of form is not tenable.
Furthermore, form that is without a cause is simply not possible at all;
therefore, one should not conceptualize any conceptual constructions regarding form.
It is not tenable that the effect is similar to the cause;
nor is it tenable that the effect is dissimilar to the cause. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 4.6)
The sequence for sensation, mind, perception, and mental formations, as well as for all entities whatsoever, is in every respect identical to that of form.
If, in the course of a debate, one should offer an avoidance based on emptiness, then everything remains unaddressed for him; it becomes equivalent to the very point yet to be proven.
If someone should offer an objection during an exposition when emptiness has been established, every such objection of theirs remains unrefuted, as it becomes equal to the very point to be proven.
Chapter Five: Examination of the Elements (Dhātuparīkṣā) Space does not exist at all prior to the characteristic of space;
for if it were to exist prior to its characteristic, it would follow that it is without characteristics. (MŚ 5.1)
Nowhere does any entity exist that is without characteristics. Since an entity without characteristics does not exist, where could a characteristic possibly apply? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 5.2)
The activity of a characteristic does not occur in that which lacks a characteristic, nor in that which possesses a characteristic;
nor does it proceed elsewhere, apart from both that which possesses a characteristic and that which lacks a characteristic.
And when the characteristic does not occur, the characterized object is not tenable;
and when the characterized object is not tenable, the characteristic itself is impossible.
Therefore, the characterized object does not exist, nor indeed does the characteristic exist;
apart from the characterized object and the characteristic, no entity exists at all.
And if an existent thing does not exist, of what will there be non-existence?
Furthermore, who, possessing the nature of neither existence nor non-existence, could perceive existence and non-existence?
Therefore, space is neither an entity nor a non-entity, neither the characterized object nor the characteristic;
the other five elements are equal to space.
But those of small intelligence who perceive existence and non-existence do not see the auspicious tranquility of all things, which is the true object of vision.

Chapter Six: An Examination of Passion and the One Who is Passionate If passion were to exist prior to the one who is passionate, it would exist independent of that person; yet passion would only exist in dependence upon him, for passion occurs only when the one who is passionate exists. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 6.1)
Furthermore, if the impassioned one does not exist, how indeed will passion come to be?
Whether passion exists or does not exist, this same sequence applies equally to the impassioned one as well.
Furthermore, it is not logical for passion and the impassioned one to arise simultaneously;
for if they were to exist thus, passion and the impassioned one would be independent of each other.
In identity, there is no coexistence, for a thing cannot coexist with itself;
in difference, moreover, how could coexistence possibly exist?
If coexistence were to exist in identity, it would exist even without a companion;
if coexistence were to exist in difference, it would exist even without a companion.
If there were coexistence in separateness, what would be established of passion and the impassioned?
For how could there be coexistence between two things whose existence is established as separate from one another?
If the separate existence of passion and the impassioned one is established,
for what purpose do you nevertheless imagine their coexistence?
Thinking that [a thing] is not established as separate, you thus desire its coexistence;
yet for the sake of establishing that coexistence, you further desire separateness.
Since separate existence is not established, coexistence is not established either.
In the presence of what kind of separate existence do you desire coexistence?
Thus, the establishment of passion by means of the impassioned is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous;
as with passion, so too is the establishment of all phenomena neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous.
7. Examination of the Conditioned (Saṃskṛtaparīkṣā), the seventh chapter.
If arising is conditioned, then the three characteristics [of the conditioned] are applicable there.
But if arising is unconditioned, how can it be a characteristic of the conditioned? (MMK 7.1)
The three [characteristics] beginning with arising, when taken separately, are not capable of performing the function of defining the conditioned;
if they were to exist together, how could they exist in one place at one time?
If there exists another characteristic of the conditioned for arising, duration, and destruction, there would be an infinite regress; if it does not exist, then they are not conditioned.
The arising of arising is merely the arising of the primary arising;
conversely, the primary arising brings about the arising of arising.
If, according to you, the "arising of arising" is the arising of the fundamental arising,
how will that [secondary arising], which has not been produced by the fundamental [arising], produce it?

If that [subsequent] fundamental [mind] produces the fundamental [mind], since it was produced by the fundamental [mind], how can that fundamental [mind], which has not yet been produced by it, produce it? (MŚ 7.6)
If this [fire], while arising, could produce that [fuel], then it would indeed produce it;
provided that this [fire], being unborn, were capable of producing it.
Just as a lamp illuminates both itself and others,
so too arising should produce both itself and others.
There is no darkness in a lamp, nor where it is situated.
What does the lamp illuminate? For illumination is the destruction of darkness.
How can darkness be destroyed by a lamp that is in the process of arising?
For at the time when the lamp is arising, it does not reach the darkness.
Or if darkness were destroyed by a lamp without even reaching it,
then a lamp situated here would destroy the darkness existing throughout the entire world.
If a lamp illuminates both itself and others,
then darkness, without a doubt, will also conceal both itself and others.
How could this arising, being itself unarisen, produce itself?
Or, if it produces while already arisen, what is produced again once it has been born?
In no way does that which is currently arising, that which has already arisen, or that which has not yet arisen arise;
this has been explained by means of the examples of the being-traversed, the traversed, and the untraversed.
When this "presently arising" does not apply to the process of arising, how can it be said that the presently arising arises in dependence upon arising? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.15)
Whatever arises dependently is, by its very nature, quiescent;
therefore, that which is arising and arising itself are both quiescent.
If some unarisen entity were found anywhere, it might arise; but since that entity does not exist, how could it arise? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.17)
If this arising, while itself arising, causes that [other] arising to arise,
then what further arising would cause that arising to arise?
If another production produces this [production], there is an infinite regress;
but if that which is unproduced is produced, then everything would be produced in that same way.
The arising of that which already exists, as well as that which does not exist, is not tenable;
nor is it tenable for that which both exists and does not exist—this has already been established previously.
The arising of an entity that is in the process of ceasing is not possible;
nor is an entity that is not in the process of ceasing possible. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.21)
An entity that has already come to rest does not rest; an entity that has not yet come to rest does not rest.
That which is currently resting does not rest; and what unarisen thing could possibly rest?
The persistence of an entity that is in the process of ceasing is not tenable;
nor is an entity that is not ceasing at all tenable. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.23)
Since all things always possess the nature of aging and death,
what things could possibly exist that are without aging and death?
The abiding of abiding by means of another abiding, or by that very same [abiding], is not tenable;
just as the arising of arising is neither by itself nor by another.
That which has not ceased does not cease, nor does that which has already ceased cease;
likewise, as for that which is currently ceasing, how could that which is unborn cease?
The cessation of an entity that is already abiding is not tenable; nor is the cessation of an entity that is not abiding tenable. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.27)
Indeed, a state is not ceased by that very same state;
nor is a state ceased by a different state. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.28)
When, in this way, the arising of all phenomena is not tenable, then, in this way, the cessation of all phenomena is also not tenable. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.29)
Furthermore, the cessation of an existent entity is not tenable;
for it is not possible for both existence and non-existence to occur in a single thing. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.30)
The cessation of even a non-existent entity is not tenable, just as the cutting off of a second head does not occur. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.31)
Cessation does not exist by way of its own self, nor does cessation exist by way of another;
just as the arising of arising is neither by way of itself nor by way of another.
Since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, the conditioned does not exist;
and since the conditioned is not established, how will the unconditioned be established? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 7.33)
Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as a city of the Gandharvas,
so have arising, enduring, and ceasing been described.
Chapter 8: Examination of the Agent and the Action A truly existent agent does not perform a truly existent action; nor does a non-existent agent strive to perform a non-existent action. (MŚ 8.1)
For that which is truly existent, there is no activity, and action would be without an agent;
for that which is truly existent, there is no activity, and the agent would be without action.
If an unreal agent were to perform an unreal action,
then the action would be without a cause, and the agent would also be without a cause.
When the cause does not exist, neither the effect nor the cause is found;
in its absence, action, the agent, and the instrument are also not found.
When actions and so forth are impossible, neither merit nor demerit exists;
and when merit and demerit do not exist, the fruit born from them does not exist.
If the fruit did not exist, the path would not lead to liberation nor to heaven; furthermore, it would follow that all purposeful actions are rendered meaningless. (MŚ 8.6)
An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not produce that which is both existent and non-existent;
for how could existence and non-existence, being mutually contradictory, exist as one?
That which is existent is not produced by that which is non-existent, nor is that which is non-existent produced by that which is existent;
for in that case, all those very same faults would necessarily follow for the agent.
An agent does not perform an action that is non-existent, nor one that is existent, nor even one that is both existent and non-existent; this is due to the very reasons previously stated.
An agent who is non-existent does not perform an action that is existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent; this is due to the very reasons previously stated.
An agent that is both existent and non-existent does not perform an action that is existent or non-existent;
one should understand that through the very reasons previously stated.
Dependent upon the agent there is the action, and dependent upon that action there is the agent;
we see no other means for their establishment.
In this way, one should understand appropriation through the relinquishing of action and the agent;
and by means of action and agent, one should analyze all remaining entities.

9. Examination of the Prior (Pūrvaparīkṣā), the Ninth Chapter: Some indeed say that he for whom seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, exist, exists prior to those [functions]. (MŚ 9.1)
For how could seeing and the other [sensory functions] belong to an entity that does not exist?
Therefore, prior to those [functions], that entity exists as established.
Furthermore, by what means is that entity which is established prior to seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, designated?
If that [self] were established even without seeing and the other [faculties],
then there is no doubt that these [faculties] would also exist without it.
Someone is manifested by something; something is manifested by someone.
How can there be someone without something? How can there be something without someone?
No one exists prior to all [the functions] such as seeing and the rest;
rather, at different times, one [function] is manifested by means of another among seeing and the rest.
If it does not exist prior to all [the functions] such as seeing and the rest, how can it exist prior to each one individually, such as seeing? (MŚ 9.7)
If that very same [self] is the seer, that very same is the hearer, and that very same is the feeler, then it would have to exist prior to each one; however, this is not tenable.
If the seer were one, the hearer another, and the knower yet another,
then while there is a seer, there would also be a hearer, and there would be a plurality of selves.
Furthermore, that [self] does not exist even in those elements from which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, arise.
If that to which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth belong, does not exist, then these [faculties] do not exist either. (MŚ 9.11)

That which does not exist prior to seeing and the other [faculties], nor at present, nor even in the future—regarding that, conceptual constructions such as "it exists" or "it does not exist" have ceased. (MŚ 9.12)
10. The Examination of Fire and Fuel, the Tenth Chapter:
If that which is the fuel were the fire, there would be identity between the agent and the object;
if the fire were other than the fuel, it would exist even without the fuel. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 10.1)
It would be eternally aflame, lacking a cause for its ignition;
furthermore, in such a case, a new commencement would be useless, and it would be devoid of action.
Because it would not depend on anything else, it would follow that [fire] is not caused by ignition;
furthermore, it would follow that what is eternally burning would be useless to rekindle. (MŚ 10.3)
In that case, if it is argued that the fuel is being ignited by this [fire], then by what is that fuel ignited when it is merely that much? (MŚ 10.4)
One who is other [than the fuel] will not attain it; one who has not attained it will not burn;
and not burning, it will not go out; or, being unextinguished, it will remain with its own characteristic.
If fire were indeed something other than fuel, it would reach the fuel, just as a woman reaches a man and a man reaches a woman. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 10.6)
Fire would indeed be something entirely other than fuel, and it might as well obtain the fuel, if fire and fuel were mutually independent of one another. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 10.7)
If fire depends on fuel, and if fuel depends on fire,
which of the two is established first, such that fire depends on it as fuel?
If fire depends on fuel as the means for establishing an already established fire, then in that case,
fuel too would exist without fire.

If an entity is established in dependence upon something else, and that very thing upon which it depends is also established [in dependence], then let that which is to be depended upon be established;
in dependence upon what, then, would what be established?
If an entity is established by depending [on something else], how can that which is not yet established depend?
On the other hand, if it is already established, its dependence is not tenable. (MŚ 10.11)
Fire does not exist in dependence on fuel, nor does fire exist without depending on fuel;
fuel does not exist in dependence on fire, nor does fuel exist without depending on fire.
Fire does not come from elsewhere, nor is fire found within the fuel;
regarding this fuel, the rest has been explained by means of [the analysis of] the being-traversed, the traversed, and the untraversed.
Furthermore, fuel is not fire, nor is fire other than fuel;
fire does not possess fuel, fuel is not in fire, nor is fire in them.
The sequence regarding the self and its appropriation has been explained by means of fire and fuel;
it applies entirely and without exception to all things, including pots, cloths, and so forth.
Those who point to a self-essence of the self and of phenomena as being distinct from one another— I do not consider them to be experts in the meaning of the teaching.

Chapter Eleven: An Examination of the Prior and Posterior Limits The Great Sage has declared that a prior limit is not known; for saṃsāra is indeed without beginning or end, having neither a first nor a last point. (MŚ 11.1)
For that which has neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle?
Therefore, in this case, the sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not occur.
If birth were to exist first and old age and death were to follow later,
then birth would be without old age and death, and one who has not died would be born.
If birth were to occur later and old age and death were at the beginning,
how could there be old age and death for that which is unborn, being without a cause?
Birth cannot logically occur simultaneously with old age and death;
for if it did, one would be dying while being born, and both would consequently be rendered causeless.
Where these sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not prevail,
how could they proliferate that birth, or its aging and death?
Effect and cause, as well as the characterized and the characteristic,
sensation and the feeler— whatever objects there may be.
Not only is a prior limit of cyclic existence not found,
but a prior limit of all existent things as well is not found.

Chapter Twelve: An Examination of Suffering. Some maintain that suffering is self-made, made by another, made by both, or without cause; yet it is not logical for suffering to be an effect [in such ways]. MŚ 12.1.
If it were self-made, it would not arise dependently;
for these very aggregates arise in dependence upon those aggregates.
If these were distinct from those, or if those were distinct from these, then suffering would be produced by another; for these [beings] would have been created by those others.
If suffering were created by one's own person, then what is that person who exists apart from suffering, by whom that suffering was self-created? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 12.4)
If suffering produced by another person is given to someone else after having been created by that other, then how could that [other] exist without suffering? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 12.5)
If suffering were produced by another person, who is that other person who, being himself devoid of suffering, creates it and sends it to another? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 12.6)
Since self-causation is not established, how could suffering be caused by another?
For if another were to produce that suffering, it would be [for him] self-caused.
Suffering is not first of all self-made, for it cannot be created by that very same [self];
nor is it other-made, for if the other were not self-made, how could suffering be made by another? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 12.8)
If suffering were produced by both [self and other] or produced by each one individually,
how could there be suffering that is neither caused by another nor caused by oneself— that is, suffering without a cause?
For it is not only that the fourfold nature of suffering does not exist;
even the fourfold nature of external entities does not exist.
Chapter 13: Examination of Conditioned Forces (Saṃskāra) "That which has the nature of deception is false," so the Blessed One has said;
and since all conditioned forces have the nature of deception, they are therefore false. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 13.1)
Whatever has the nature of being deceptive is false; what is it therein that is deceived?
This was stated by the Blessed One as an elucidation of emptiness.
The lack of intrinsic nature in entities is established because change is observed;
for there is no entity that lacks intrinsic nature, since all entities are empty.
If intrinsic nature does not exist, of what could there be alteration?
If intrinsic nature does exist, of what could there be alteration? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 13.4)
Neither the change of that very thing nor the change of something else is tenable;
for a youth does not age, and one who has already aged does not age.
If there were a transformation of that [milk], then milk itself would be curd;
or else, what other thing besides milk could become curd? (MŚ 13.6)
If there were something non-empty, then there might be something called "empty.
But since there is nothing whatsoever that is non-empty, how will there be an empty?
Emptiness was taught by the Victors as the relinquishing of all views;
but those for whom emptiness itself is a view were declared incurable.
Chapter Fourteen: Examination of Contact The object of vision, the act of seeing, and the seer—these three do not enter into contact with one another either two by two or all together. (MMK 14.1)
In this way, let passion, the one who is impassioned, and the object of passion be seen;
by this threefold division, so too are the remaining afflictions and the remaining sense-bases.
The conjunction of one thing with another presupposes their distinctness;
yet that distinctness does not exist among the objects of sight and so forth, because they do not enter into conjunction.
Not only does otherness not exist for the seer and so forth;
otherness is not logically tenable for anything whatsoever in relation to anything else.
One thing arises in dependence on another; one thing does not exist apart from another.
Since B arises in dependence on A, it is therefore not tenable that B is other than A.
If one thing were other than another even without [depending on] that other, then that other would exist as other without the other; yet it does not so exist, and therefore it does not exist.
Otherness does not exist in that which is other, nor does it exist in that which is not other.
Since otherness does not exist, there is neither "other" nor "that very thing."
Neither the mixing of that with itself nor the mixing of one thing with another is possible;
for neither the process of mixing, the mixed entity, nor the mixer exists.
Chapter 15: Examination of Intrinsic Nature (Svabhāvaparīkṣā) The arising of intrinsic nature through causes and conditions is not logical.
If intrinsic nature were produced from causes and conditions, it would be something created. (MMK 15.1)
Furthermore, how could intrinsic nature (svabhāva) possibly be something produced?
For intrinsic nature is uncreated and independent of anything else. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 15.2)
How can there be an other-nature (parabhāva) when intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is absent?
For intrinsic nature is said to be the other-nature of an other-nature. (MŚ 15.3)
Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, how could an entity exist?
For an entity is established only when there is either intrinsic nature or extrinsic nature.
If existence is not established, non-existence is certainly not established;
for people describe non-existence as the alteration of existence.
Those who perceive intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, as well as existence and non-existence, do not perceive the reality in the Buddha’s teaching.
And in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" were refuted by the Blessed One, who discerns both existence and non-existence.
If existence were by way of intrinsic nature, its non-existence would not occur;
for a change in the state of intrinsic nature is never possible.
If intrinsic nature does not exist, of what could there be alteration?
And if intrinsic nature exists, of what could there be alteration? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 15.9)
"To say 'it exists' is the grasping at eternalism; to say 'it does not exist' is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, the wise person should not rely upon either existence or non-existence."
For that which exists by way of intrinsic nature cannot be non-existent; thus, eternalism follows.
To say "it does not exist now though it existed previously" entails the consequence of nihilism.
Chapter 16: Examination of Bondage and Liberation If it is held that the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) transmigrate, they do not transmigrate if they are permanent;
nor do they transmigrate if they are impermanent. This same reasoning applies to a sentient being (*sattva*) as well.
If a person transmigrates within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, that person cannot be found in any of the five ways; since he does not exist, who is it that will transmigrate?
Transmigrating from one appropriation to another, one would become non-existent;
and being non-existent and without appropriation, who is that [person], and what will transmigrate?
The nirvana of conditioned phenomena is not possible in any way;
likewise, the nirvana of a sentient being is also not possible in any way.
Formations, being subject to the nature of arising and passing away, are neither bound nor liberated;
as before, a sentient being is neither bound nor liberated.
If grasping is the bondage, then one who possesses grasping is not bound;
nor is one without grasping bound. In what state, then, is one bound?
One might wish to bind that which has not yet been bound, provided it existed prior to being bound;
but that does not exist, as has already been explained regarding the present process of going, the gone, and the not-yet-gone.
One who is bound is not liberated, nor indeed is one who is unbound liberated.
If the bound were being liberated, there would be simultaneous binding and liberation.
"I shall attain nirvāṇa without grasping; nirvāṇa will be mine"—for those who hold such a view, this is a great grasping at clinging.
There is no superimposition of nirvāṇa, nor any removal of saṃsāra.
Where [these do not exist], what is saṃsāra there, or what nirvāṇa is conceptualized?

Chapter Seventeen: An Examination of Action and its Fruit That mind which restrains oneself and benefits others—that is loving-kindness (*maitra*); it is the Dharma, the seed of fruit both in this world and after death. (MŚ 17.1)
The Supreme Seer has stated that action consists of volition and what is performed after having willed;
he has fully proclaimed many varieties of this action.
In that regard, what is called "volition" (cetanā) is known as mental action;
and what is called "having willed" (cetayitvā) is both bodily and vocal action.
The movement of speech and the non-abstinences which are designated as non-informative,
as well as other non-informative states, are likewise considered abstinences.
Merit resulting from enjoyment, demerit of the same kind,
and volition— these seven factors are known as the manifestations of karma.
If the action were to persist until the time of ripening, it would attain the status of being eternal;
if, however, it has ceased, how can that which has ceased produce a fruit?
The continuum beginning with the sprout that proceeds from the seed—without that seed, it would not proceed. From that [continuum], the fruit arises. MŚ 17.7.
Since the continuum arises from the seed, and the production of the fruit arises from the continuum, the fruit is preceded by the seed; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
The mental continuum which proceeds from that mind—its fruit arises from that; yet, without the mind, it does not proceed.
Since the continuum arises from the mind, and the arising of the fruit arises from the continuum,
the fruit preceded by karma is therefore neither annihilated nor eternal.
The ten white paths of action are the means for accomplishing the Dharma;
the fruit of the Dharma consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure, both in this world and after death.
Furthermore, many and great faults would arise even from this conceptual construction;
therefore, this conceptual construction is not at all tenable here.
Furthermore, I shall now set forth this conceptualization which is applicable here,
and which has been praised by the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas.
Just as a promissory note is indestructible, so too are debt and karma;
it is fourfold according to its constituent elements, and by nature it is indeterminate.
It is not to be abandoned by the path of seeing, nor is it to be abandoned by the path of cultivation;
therefore, the fruit of actions arises through non-perishing.
If [an action] were to be abandoned through its relinquishment or by the transference of karma,
then faults such as the destruction of karma would follow.
At the moment of rebirth, among all the homogeneous and heterogeneous karmas belonging to the same realm, only one of them arises.
That [result] arises from every kind of action—whether of two types—in the present life; and it remains even when [the action] has ripened.
It ceases either through the transcendence of its fruit or through death;
therein one should discern the distinction between that which is with outflows and that which is without outflows.
Emptiness is not annihilation, and cyclic existence is not eternal;
the non-perishing of karma—this is the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Why does karma not arise? Because it is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). And because it is unarisen, it does not perish. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 17.21)
If karma were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature, it would undoubtedly be eternal;
moreover, karma would be uncreated, for that which is eternal is never produced.
If action were uncreated, there would be the fear of encountering the results of what one has not done;
furthermore, the fault of not living the holy life (abrahmacaryavāsa) would follow in that case.
All worldly conventions would undoubtedly be contradicted;
furthermore, the distinction between the doer of merit and the doer of evil would not be tenable. (MŚ 17.24)
Furthermore, that which has already ripened as its maturation would ripen yet again;
for if action were established by way of intrinsic nature, it would necessarily be so.
This [world] consists of karma and afflictions (kleśa), yet those afflictions do not exist in reality.
If those afflictions do not exist in reality, how could karma exist in reality? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 17.26)
Karma and the afflictions are declared to be the conditions for bodies;
if karma and the afflictions are empty, what can be said of the bodies?
Enshrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, that living being is the enjoyer; yet he is neither other than the agent nor is he that very same person.
Since this action does not arise from conditions, nor is it produced without conditions,
therefore the agent also does not exist.
If there is no action and no agent, how could there be a fruit born of action?
And if the fruit does not exist, how indeed will there be an enjoyer?
Just as the Teacher, through his perfection of supernatural power, creates an emanation,
and that emanation in turn creates another emanation, and that emanation again [creates yet another].
In the same way, the agent and the action performed by him have the form of a magical creation;
just as one magical creation is created by another magical creation, so it is.
Afflictions, actions, bodies, agents, and fruits are like the city of the Gandharvas; they resemble a mirage or a dream.

18. Examination of the Self, the Eighteenth Chapter. If the self were the aggregates, it would be subject to arising and passing away. If it were other than the aggregates, it would lack the characteristics of the aggregates. (MMK 18.1)
When the self does not exist, how indeed could that which belongs to the self exist?
Through the pacification of both the self and what pertains to the self, one is free from "mine-ness" and free from "I-ness."
That which is without "mine-ness" and without "I-ness" does not exist either;
he who perceives that which is without "mine-ness" and without "I-ness" does not perceive.
When "mine" and "I" have perished, both externally and internally, grasping ceases;
through the destruction of that, there is the destruction of birth.
Liberation comes from the exhaustion of karma and afflictions; karma and afflictions arise from conceptual construction;
these arise from mental proliferation; but mental proliferation ceases in emptiness.
The Buddhas have designated "self," they have taught "non-self," and they have also taught that there is neither self nor non-self whatsoever.
When the range of the mind has ceased, that which is to be designated ceases;
for the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither arisen nor ceased, like nirvāṇa.
"Everything is real, or not real, both real and unreal, and neither unreal nor real—this is the instruction of the Buddhas. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 18.8)
Not dependent on another, peaceful, not proliferated by conceptual proliferations, free from discursive thought, and without manifold meanings— this is the characteristic of reality.
Whatever arises dependently is not indeed that very thing, nor is it something other than it;
therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Neither having multiple meanings nor having diverse meanings, neither annihilated nor eternal—
this is the nectar of the teaching of the Buddhas, the Lords of the World.
When the fully enlightened Buddhas have not appeared and the Śrāvakas have passed away,
the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas arises from solitude.

Chapter 19: Examination of Time, the Nineteenth Treatise. If the present and the future exist in dependence upon the past, then the present and the future would both exist within the time that is the past. (MMK 19.1)
If, moreover, the present and the future do not exist there [in the past],
how could the present and the future exist in dependence upon it?
Furthermore, the establishment of those two [past and future] does not exist without depending on the past;
therefore, neither the present nor the future time exists.
By this very same [method], one should characterize the two remaining types of exchange in their proper order—the superior, inferior, and middling, as well as unity and so forth. (MŚ 19.4)
Time that is not abiding cannot be grasped, and abiding time does not exist.
How can time be designated if it is neither being grasped nor has been grasped?
If time exists in dependence upon an entity, how can there be time apart from an entity?
Since no entity whatsoever exists, how will time come to be?

20. Examination of the Collection (Sāmagrīparīkṣā), the Twentieth Chapter If the fruit arises from the collection of causes and conditions, and if that fruit already exists within the collection, how can it arise from the collection?
If the fruit arises from the assemblage of causes and conditions,
and yet that fruit does not exist within the assemblage, how can it arise from the assemblage?
If the effect exists within the assemblage of causes and conditions, it should indeed be perceived within that assemblage;
yet it is not perceived within the assemblage.
If the effect does not exist within the assemblage of causes and conditions,
then those causes and conditions would be equivalent to non-causes and non-conditions.
If the cause, having given its causal efficiency to the fruit, were then to cease, then the cause would possess a twofold nature:
that which has been given and that which has ceased.
If the cause were to cease without having imparted its causal efficiency to the fruit,
then that fruit, having arisen when the cause has ceased, would be without a cause.
If, moreover, the fruit were to manifest simultaneously with the causal complex,
it would follow that the producer and that which is produced exist at the same time.
Furthermore, if the fruit were to manifest prior to the causal complex itself,
then the fruit would be devoid of causes and conditions, and thus would be causeless.
If the fruit were to exist when the cause has already ceased, there would be a transference of the cause;
furthermore, it would follow that a cause already previously born would be born again.
How could a cause that has ceased and come to an end produce an arisen effect?
And even if it were to persist, how could the cause produce the effect while being enveloped by it?
Now, if this [cause] were unobstructed by its fruit, what kind of fruit could it produce?
For a cause does not produce a fruit either by not seeing it or by seeing it.
For a past effect, there is never found any conjunction with a past cause,
nor with one that is unborn, nor with one that has already arisen.
For there is never any conjunction of an arisen effect with an unarisen cause, nor with one that is past, nor with one that has already arisen. (MŚ 20.13)
For there is never any conjunction of an unarisen effect with a cause that has arisen, nor with one that is unarisen, nor with one that has perished. (MŚ 20.14)
If there is no conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect?
Or, if there is a conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 20.15)
If the cause is empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect?
If the cause is not empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 20.16)
A non-empty fruit will not arise, and a non-empty one will not cease.
That which is non-empty would thus be neither ceased nor arisen.
How can that which is empty arise? How can that which is empty cease?
It follows that even the empty would be unceased and unarisen.
The identity of cause and effect is never tenable;
nor indeed is the difference between cause and effect ever tenable.
If cause and effect were identical, there would be oneness between the producer and the produced;
if cause and effect were distinct, a cause would be equivalent to a non-cause. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 20.20)
How will a cause produce an effect that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature? How will a cause produce an effect that does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature? (MŚ 20.21)
And the status of being a cause is not tenable for that which does not produce;
and if the status of being a cause is untenable, of what will there be a fruit?
Furthermore, how could that very collection of conditions and causes, which by itself does not produce its own self, produce an effect? (MŚ 20.23)
The fruit is not produced by the causal complex, nor is the fruit produced by what is not a causal complex;
since there is no causal complex without a fruit, how indeed can the fruit exist?

Chapter Twenty-One: An Examination of Origination and Dissolution Dissolution does not exist either apart from or together with origination; nor indeed does origination exist either apart from or together with dissolution. (MMK 21.1)
How indeed could there be dissolution without origination? There can be no death without birth; dissolution does not exist without emergence.
How could passing away exist simultaneously with arising?
For birth and death cannot be found at the same time.
How indeed could there be arising without passing away?
For impermanence is never absent from existing things.
How can arising exist together with passing away?
For birth and death are not found to occur at the same time.
If for two things there is no establishment either together with one another or without one another, how indeed can their establishment exist?
There is no arising of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there the arising of that which is not subject to destruction;
there is no passing away of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there the passing away of that which is not subject to destruction.
Neither origination nor cessation exists without an entity;
neither an entity nor its cessation exists without origination and cessation.
Neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is empty;
neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is non-empty.
It is not tenable that origination and dissolution are one and the same;
nor is it tenable that origination and dissolution are different.
Both arising and passing away would be perceived by you;
yet it is only through delusion that both arising and passing away are perceived.
An existent does not arise from an existent, nor does an existent arise from a non-existent;
a non-existent does not arise from a non-existent, nor does a non-existent arise from an existent.
An entity is not born from itself, nor is it born from another;
it is not born from both itself and another.
From what, then, could it be born?
For one who accepts the existence of an entity, the views of eternalism or nihilism necessarily follow;
for that entity must be either permanent or impermanent.
For one who has accepted [the principle of] becoming, there is neither annihilation nor permanence;
for that "becoming" is indeed the continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and fruit.
If that existence (bhava) were a continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect,
it would follow that there is a total severance of the cause, because what has passed away does not arise again.
It is not logical for that which exists by way of its own intrinsic nature to become non-existent;
furthermore, at the time of nirvāṇa, there would be annihilation due to the cessation of the continuum of existence.
The first existence is not tenable when the last has ceased;
nor is the first existence tenable when the last has not ceased.
If the first were to arise while the last is ceasing,
then one would be in the process of ceasing and the other would be in the process of arising.
If it were not the case that the process of ceasing and the process of arising are joined together, then one would be born within those very aggregates in which one dies. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 21.20)
Thus, the continuity of existence is not tenable in any of the three times;
how can that which does not exist in the three times be a continuity of existence?
Chapter 22: Examination of the Tathāgata The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he other than the aggregates; the aggregates are not in him, nor is he in them.
The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates; who, then, is the Tathāgata here?
If the Buddha does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) based upon the aggregates,
how can he exist by way of extrinsic nature (parabhāva), he who does not exist by way of intrinsic nature?
That which exists in dependence upon another nature is established as being without self;
and how can that which is without self be the Tathāgata?
If intrinsic nature does not exist, how could extrinsic nature exist?
Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, who is that Tathāgata?
If some Tathāgata were to exist without depending on the aggregates, he would now have to depend on them; therefore, he would exist by means of dependence.
Without depending upon the aggregates, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever;
and how can that which does not exist without depending [on them] ever come to depend [upon them]?
There is no appropriation whatsoever that is not appropriated,
nor does a Tathāgata exist in any way whatsoever without appropriation.
How can that Tathāgata be designated by means of appropriation, when he does not exist as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], even when sought in five ways?
This appropriation, too, does not exist because it lacks intrinsic nature;
and how could that which does not exist by way of its own nature exist by way of another nature? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 22.9)
Thus, grasping and the grasper are entirely empty; yet, by means of that which is empty, [the Tathāgata] is designated. How, then, can the Tathāgata be empty?
"One should not say 'it is empty,' nor that 'it is non-empty'; nor both, nor neither. It is spoken of, however, for the purpose of conventional designation. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 22.11)

How can the fourfold [views] beginning with eternalism and non-eternalism exist in that which is peaceful? And how can the fourfold [views] beginning with finitude and infinity exist here in that which is peaceful? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 22.12)
He who has grasped the dense notion that the Tathāgata exists,
by conceptualizing that he does not exist, would likewise conceptualize him even after his parinirvāṇa.
Since this [Buddha] is empty by its very nature, the thought that "the Buddha exists after cessation" or "he does not exist" is simply not tenable.
Those who conceptualize the Buddha, who is beyond conceptual proliferation and undecaying, are all destroyed by conceptual proliferation; they do not see the Tathāgata.
Whatever is the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata, that is the intrinsic nature of this world;
the Tathāgata is without intrinsic nature, and this world is without intrinsic nature.
23. Examination of Error (Viparyāsaparīkṣā), the twenty-third chapter.
Passion, hatred, and delusion are said to originate from conceptual construction;
for they arise in dependence upon the errors regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant. (MMK 23.1)
Those afflictions which arise in dependence upon the beautiful, the ugly, and the inversions do not exist by way of their own nature; therefore, the afflictions do not exist in reality.
The existence and non-existence of the self are not established in any way whatsoever;
without that [self], how could the existence and non-existence of the afflictions be established? (MŚ 23.3)
For these afflictions belong to someone, yet that "someone" is not established; or rather, do the afflictions exist without anyone to whom they belong? They do not belong to anyone.
As with the view of a self-body, the afflictions do not exist in the afflicted in five ways;
as with the view of a self-body, the afflicted also does not exist in the afflictions in five ways.
Intrinsic nature does not exist for the errors of purity and impurity;
dependent upon what errors of purity and impurity could the afflictions arise?
Visible forms, sounds, tastes, tangibles, odors, and mental phenomena— these sixfold objects are conceptually constructed as the basis for attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Forms, sounds, tastes, touches, smells,
and mental phenomena alone are like the city of the Gandharvas, resembling a mirage or a dream.
How could there be either impurity or purity in those things which are like illusory persons and equal to reflections? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 23.9)
Without depending on the beautiful, we could not designate the ugly;
since the beautiful exists in dependence [upon it], therefore the beautiful is not at all tenable.
Without depending on the impure, we could not designate the pure;
since the impure exists in dependence upon that [pure], therefore the impure does not exist at all.
And when the pleasant does not exist, from where will passion arise?
And when the unpleasant does not exist, from where will aversion arise? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 23.12)
If the grasping at the impermanent as permanent is a perversion,
then since nothing impermanent exists in emptiness, how can there be such a grasping or perversion?
If the grasping at the permanent in the impermanent is a misconception,
why is the grasping at "impermanent" not also a misconception regarding the empty?
That by which one grasps, that which is the grasping, the grasper, and that which is grasped—all these are utterly tranquil; therefore, no grasping exists.
If grasping does not exist— whether it be false or even correct—
to whom would there be error, and to whom would there be non-error?
Furthermore, errors do not occur for one who is already mistaken,
nor do errors occur for one who is not mistaken.
Errors do not occur for one who is currently undergoing error;
reflect for yourself as to whose errors could possibly occur.
How indeed could errors exist if they have not arisen? If errors have not been born, how can there be one who has fallen into error?
An entity is not born from itself, nor is it born from another;
it is not born from both self and other—how, then, can one who has fallen into such views be subject to error?
If a self that is pure, eternal, and blissful exists, then the self would not be a misconception as being pure, eternal, and blissful. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 23.21)
If neither a self, nor purity, nor permanence, nor happiness exists, then neither non-self, nor impurity, nor impermanence, nor suffering exists either. (MŚ 23.22)
In this way, ignorance ceases through the cessation of its inversions;
when ignorance has ceased, the formative forces and the rest cease as well.
If any afflictions whatsoever were to exist for anyone by way of intrinsic nature, how indeed could they be abandoned? Who can abandon intrinsic nature?
If any afflictions whatsoever were non-existent by way of their own nature for anyone, how indeed could they be abandoned? Who would abandon that which has no real existence?
24. Examination of the Noble Truths, the Twenty-fourth Chapter.
If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away;
it follows for you that the four noble truths do not exist. (MMK 24.1)
Full comprehension, abandonment, cultivation,
and realization would not be possible due to the non-existence of the four noble truths.
In the absence of that [the path], the four noble fruits do not exist;
and in the absence of the fruits, there are neither those who abide in the fruits nor those who have entered toward them.
If those eight types of persons do not exist, then the Saṅgha does not exist;
and due to the non-existence of the Noble Truths, the True Dharma also does not exist.
If the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha?
By speaking thus, you deny all three Jewels.
By [asserting] emptiness, you subvert the existence of the fruits, as well as non-dharma and dharma itself,
and all worldly conventions.
To this we reply: You do not understand the purpose of emptiness, nor emptiness itself, nor the meaning of emptiness; therefore you are thus frustrated. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.7)
The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate meaning.
Those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths do not understand the profound reality in the Buddha’s teaching. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.9)
Without relying upon conventional usage, the ultimate truth is not taught;
without attaining the ultimate truth, nirvāṇa is not realized.
Emptiness, when wrongly perceived, destroys the person of dull intellect, just as a snake poorly grasped or a spell incorrectly cast. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.11)
And for this reason, the Sage turned his mind away from teaching the Dharma,
considering that this Dharma is difficult for the dull-witted to penetrate.
Furthermore, as for the objection you raise regarding the over-extension [of the principle] to emptiness,
that consequence of a fault does not apply to us in respect to the empty.
Everything is logical for him for whom emptiness is logical;
nothing is logical for him for whom emptiness is not logical.
Thus, while casting upon us the faults that belong to yourself,
you have mounted the horse itself and yet have forgotten the horse.
If you perceive the existence of things by way of their intrinsic nature,
then you perceive those things as being without causes and conditions.
You negate both effect and cause, as well as the agent, the instrument, and the action;
you negate arising and ceasing, and the fruit as well.
That which is dependent origination, we declare to be emptiness;
it is a dependent designation, and it is itself the middle way.
Since no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not dependently originated,
therefore no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is non-empty.
If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
it would follow that, for you, the four noble truths do not exist.
How could there be suffering that is not dependently originated?
For it has been stated that suffering is impermanent; indeed, such [suffering] does not exist if it possesses intrinsic nature.
What more could possibly arise from that which already exists by way of its own nature?
Therefore, for one who contradicts emptiness, there is no origination.
The cessation of suffering that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not possible;
by asserting the existence of intrinsic nature, you obstruct cessation.
If the path possesses intrinsic nature, its cultivation is not tenable;
yet if that path is cultivated, for you, intrinsic nature does not exist.
When suffering, its origin, and its cessation do not exist, what path, by virtue of being the cessation of suffering, will bring about [that cessation]? (MŚ 24.25)
If there is non-comprehension by way of intrinsic nature, how could there be comprehension of it again?
For indeed, intrinsic nature is said to be eternally established.
In that case, for you, abandonment, realization, and cultivation would likewise not be tenable, nor would the four fruits [of the spiritual life] exist, just as thorough knowledge does not.
Furthermore, how could a fruit that has not been attained by way of intrinsic nature ever be attained by one who grasps at intrinsic nature? Mś 24.28.
If there is no fruit, then those established in the fruits do not exist, nor do those who have entered toward them;
if these eight types of persons do not exist, then the Saṅgha does not exist.
And because the noble truths do not exist, the True Dharma also does not exist;
when the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha? (MŚ 24.30)

Furthermore, it would follow for you that enlightenment exists independently of a Buddha, and it would also follow for you that a Buddha exists independently of enlightenment. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.31)
And whoever is by nature unawakened, even though striving for awakening,
will not attain awakening through the conduct of a bodhisattva.
And no one will ever perform either dharma or adharma; for what can be done with that which is non-empty? Indeed, intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not something that can be produced.
Indeed, for you, there exists a fruit even without dharma and adharma;
yet for you, there exists no fruit that has dharma and adharma as its cause.
Or if you hold that there is a fruit caused by merit and demerit, how can that fruit, produced from merit and demerit, be non-empty for you? (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.35)
And you contradict all worldly conventions because you contradict emptiness, which is dependent origination.
Nothing at all would need to be done, and action would be uninitiated;
one who negates emptiness would be an agent without acting. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.37)
The world will be unarisen, unceased, and immutable;
though it appears through various states, it is devoid of intrinsic nature.
If things were not empty, there would be no attainment of what has not yet been attained, no action that brings an end to suffering, and no abandonment of all afflictions.
Whoever sees dependent origination sees this:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path itself.
25. Examination of Nirvāṇa, the Twenty-fifth Chapter If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away. Through the abandoning or the cessation of what is nirvāṇa intended? (MMK 25.1)
If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
through the abandoning or the cessation of what, then, is nirvāṇa intended?
That which is neither abandoned nor attained, neither annihilated nor eternal,
neither ceased nor arisen— this is called nirvāṇa.

First of all, nirvāṇa cannot be an existent thing, for it would follow that it possesses the characteristics of aging and death; indeed, there is no existent thing that exists without aging and death.
And if nirvāṇa were an existent entity, then nirvāṇa would be conditioned;
for no existent entity whatsoever exists anywhere that is unconditioned.
And if nirvāṇa were an entity, how could it be non-dependent?
For no entity whatsoever exists that is not dependent.
If nirvāṇa is not an existent, what will non-existence be?
In that nirvāṇa where no existent exists, no non-existent exists either.
If nirvana were a non-entity, how could it be non-dependent?
For there exists no such thing as a non-entity that occurs independently of anything else.
That which is the state of coming and going, depending upon and conditioned by [causes],
is taught as Nirvana when it is neither conditioned nor dependent.
The Teacher has declared the abandonment of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence.
If nirvāṇa were both existence and non-existence, then liberation would be both existence and non-existence; and that is not tenable.
If nirvāṇa were both an entity and a non-entity, then nirvāṇa would not be non-dependent;
for that [nirvāṇa] would consist of both, which are dependent.
How could nirvāṇa be both existence and non-existence?
For nirvāṇa is unconditioned, whereas existence and non-existence are conditioned.
How could both non-existence and existence exist in nirvāṇa?
For the non-existence of these two in a single place is like that of light and darkness.
The teaching that "nirvāṇa is neither non-existence nor existence" is established only if both existence and non-existence are themselves established.
If nirvāṇa exists as neither non-existence nor existence,
by what is it characterized as "neither non-existence nor existence"?
It cannot be conceived that the Blessed One exists after cessation;
nor can it be conceived that he does not exist, or both, or neither.
Even while remaining, the Blessed One is not conceived as "existing";
he is not conceived as "not existing," nor as "both," nor as "neither."
There is no distinction whatsoever between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
there is no distinction whatsoever between nirvāṇa and saṃsāra. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 25.19)
The limit of nirvāṇa and the limit of saṃsāra—
between these two, not even the slightest difference is found.
Furthermore, views concerning the end and so forth, as well as those concerning eternity and so forth, depend upon nirvāṇa, the future limit, and the past limit. (MŚ 25.21)
Since all phenomena are empty, what is infinite? What is finite?
What is both infinite and finite? And what is neither infinite nor finite?
Is it that very same thing? Is it something else? Is it eternal? Is it non-eternal?
Is it both non-eternal and eternal? Or is it neither of these two?
The cessation of all apprehension, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, is auspicious.
No dharma whatsoever has been taught by the Buddha anywhere to anyone.
Chapter 26: Examination of the Twelve Links.
One who is obscured by ignorance performs three kinds of formative forces for the sake of renewed existence;
by means of those karmas, one goes to a state of rebirth. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 26.1)
Consciousness, conditioned by formative forces, descends into the realm of rebirth;
once consciousness has descended, name-and-form is infused.
When name-and-form has been infused, however, the six sense bases arise;
having reached the six sense bases, contact comes into being.
Depending upon the eye, visible forms, and attention,
as well as depending upon name-and-form, consciousness thus comes into being.
The conjunction of these three—the eye, form, and consciousness—is contact;
from that contact, feeling arises.
Craving has feeling as its condition, for one craves for the sake of feeling;
while craving, one grasps at the fourfold grasping.
When there is grasping, existence proceeds for the grasper;
for if one were without grasping, one would be liberated and existence would not come to be.
Those five aggregates are existence (bhava); from existence, birth proceeds;
and from birth come old age, death, suffering, and so forth, along with sorrow and lamentation.
Mental distress and despair proceed from this birth;
thus occurs the arising of this entire mass of suffering.
Therefore, it is the ignorant person who constructs the formative forces (saṃskāra) which are the root of saṃsāra;
thus, the ignorant one is the agent, whereas the wise one is not, because of his vision of reality.
When ignorance has ceased, there is the non-arising of formative forces;
the cessation of ignorance, however, results from the cultivation of this very knowledge.
Through the cessation of each respective [condition], that very [effect] does not proceed;
thus this entire mass of suffering is completely extinguished.

Chapter 27: Examination of Views The views that "I existed in past time" or "I did not exist," as well as those views concerning the eternity of the world and so forth, are all based upon the prior limit [of existence]. (MMK 27.1)
The views such as "I shall not exist" and "Shall I exist as something else in the future time," as well as those beginning with "the end," are based upon the posterior limit.
"It was not" in past time—this is not tenable;
for he who existed in previous births is not this very same person.
If it were the case that "that very [appropriation] is the self," then the appropriation would be distinguished [as the self].
But then, what indeed is your self when it is completely separated from appropriation?
If it is maintained that there is no self apart from the appropriated aggregates,
then for you it would follow that the appropriated aggregates themselves are the self, yet you also maintain that the self does not exist.
Furthermore, appropriation itself is not the self, for that [appropriation] passes away and arises again.
How indeed could appropriation be the appropriator?
Furthermore, a self that is distinct from the appropriation is not at all tenable;
for if it were distinct, it would be perceived as being without appropriation, yet it is not so perceived.
Thus, the self is neither other than the appropriation nor is it the appropriation itself; there is no self without appropriation, yet it is not certain that it does not exist.
"It was not the case that I existed in past time"—this is not tenable;
for this [present person] is not other than that [person] in previous births. (MŚ 27.9)
For if this [person] were other [than the aggregates], he would exist even after rejecting them;
likewise, he would remain there as he was, or he would be born there immortal.
The annihilation of actions, the destruction of actions performed by one person, and the enjoyment of those actions by another—such consequences as these would follow. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 27.11)
Nor has it arisen without having previously existed, for in that case a logical fault would follow:
either the self would be something created, or it would have come into being without a cause. (MŚ 27.12)
Thus, regarding the past, the view that "I existed," "I did not exist," "both," or "neither" is not tenable.
The view, "Will I indeed exist in the future time?
and "I will not exist"—these are the same as [the analysis] regarding the past time.
If that god were also a human being, he would be eternal;
yet the god would be unarisen, for that which is eternal is not born.
If the human were other than the god, then there would be impermanence;
if the human were other than the god, then continuity would not be possible.
If one part were divine and another part human, it would be both non-eternal and eternal; and that is not tenable.
If both the non-eternal and the eternal were established, then indeed the eternal would be established, as would the non-eternal. (MMK 27.18)
If someone had come from somewhere and were to go again to somewhere else, then saṃsāra would be beginningless; but such a person does not exist. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 27.19)
If there exists nothing that is eternal, what could there be that is non-eternal?
And how could there be both the eternal and the non-eternal, or that which is excluded from both of these?
If the world were finite, how could there be a future life?
Moreover, if the world were infinite, how could there be a future life?
Since this continuum of the aggregates proceeds like the flame of a lamp, therefore neither finitude nor infinitude is tenable.
If the prior aggregates were to perish and these [present] aggregates were not to arise in dependence upon those aggregates, then the world would be finite.
If these aggregates had not been destroyed in the past, nor had they arisen,
then this world would be infinite by depending upon these aggregates.
If one part were finite while another part were infinite, the world would be both finite and infinite; but that is not tenable.
How, first of all, could one part of the appropriator perish while another part does not perish? This is not tenable.
How indeed could one part of the appropriation perish while another part does not perish? This too is not tenable.
If both the finite and the infinite were established as real, then it would be established that [the world] is neither finite nor infinite, according to your desire. (MŚ 27.28)
Alternatively, since all things are empty, where, for whom, which, and from what cause could views such as eternalism and the rest possibly arise?
I pay homage to Gautama, who, out of compassion, taught the true Dharma for the sake of abandoning all views.
